1.pericope_label: Every wise woman buildeth her house: in the mouth of the foolish is a rod of pride: where no oxen are, the crib is clean: a faithful witness will not lie

schools.summary: Henry describes the prudent wife who makes a family prosper while knowing the rule belongs to her husband, and observes that many a family is ruined by ill housewifery as well as by ill husbandry; he makes the rod of pride a branch from the root of bitterness in the heart, so that the proud man’s tongue becomes a rod for his own back; and he finds the joke in the clean crib, which pleases the nice who cannot endure the dirty work of husbandry and sell their oxen to keep it clean, though the dung of the ox is wanted as well as his labour.

Gill takes the Wisdom of the first verse for Christ, who in this book goes by that name and builds his house upon himself, notes that the word for clean in the fourth verse is elsewhere used for wheat so that the line may mean the granary is without corn, and applies the scorner of the sixth to those who sought wisdom in the wrong way and found none.

Clarke makes the building of the house material, an increase of property and food, and defends the ox against the horse point by point, as longer lived, scarcely liable to disease, steady in his gears, kept at a third of the cost, more profitable in his manure, and useful in flesh and horn and hide when worn out; he also keeps the rod of pride to the manner of such reproofs, ill-judged and ill-timed; Wesley makes the insolent speeches a rod for their own backs and recalls that cleanness of teeth stands elsewhere for famine.

Ellicott renders the first verse as the wisdom of women building for each her house, reverses the second so that he who fears the Lord walks in his uprightness, allows both senses of the rod of pride, and takes the fourth verse either as an exhortation to kindness towards animals or as an observation that labour has its disagreeable side and its reward; Keil and Delitzsch argue at length against the rendering the wise among women, work on a word for the switch that occurs elsewhere only once, report two renderings of an earlier translator and object that a sceptre would need another word, and read the fourth verse as a commendation of cattle-breeding carrying an admonition to treat the ox gently.

debates: How should the first verse be construed? Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both prefer abstracts, the wisdom of women building and their folly pulling down, rather than a wise woman and a foolish one. Keil and Delitzsch argue it from the language: if the wise among women were meant the plain phrase used elsewhere would be expected, the individualising verb that follows is against it, and the abstract folly in the second half suggests a like abstract in the first, though three versions write a wise woman and one scholar treats the word as an adjective. Henry, Clarke, Gill and Wesley pass the question by and expound the woman.
outliers: Clarke defends the ox against the horse in six numbered points, from length of life and freedom from disease to the use of his hide and horns after death.
Henry finds the irony of the fourth verse in its cleanness, since the crib is clean of dung, which pleases those too nice for husbandry, though the dung of the ox is wanted as well as his labour.

Keil and Delitzsch report an earlier translator’s two attempts at the rod of pride, that fools speak tyrannically and that the fool has the sceptre of pride, and object that a sceptre would have required another word.
Ellicott reverses the second verse, so that it states not that the upright walker fears the Lord but that he who fears the Lord walks uprightly.
themes: a wise woman or the wisdom of women
a switch, not a sceptre
the ox weighed against the horse
a crib clean because it is empty
fear that shows itself in walking

7.pericope_label: Go from the presence of a foolish man: the wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way: fools make a mock at sin: the heart knoweth his own bitterness: the house of the wicked shall be overthrown: there is a way which seemeth right unto a man

schools.summary: Henry makes the second half of the seventh verse a test for discovering a fool, since a discourse with no relish or savour of piety shows the treasure is bad, and says that sometimes the only way of reproving wicked discourse is to leave the company; he insists the wisdom of the prudent is practical and not the speculation of the learned, since we are travellers whose concern is to get forward and not to spy wonders; he holds that those who make light of sin make light of Christ; and he warns that we must not censure the griefs of others, whose stroke is perhaps heavier than their groaning.

Gill reads the seventh verse as a plain command to shun a wicked man as dangerous and infectious, takes the way of the prudent as the way of a man’s calling, duty and salvation, reports that some render the word of the ninth verse a sin offering and turns that against those who displace the offering of Christ, and notes that bitterness of soul is not every heart’s case, since a man may be in the gall of bitterness and feel nothing of it.

Clarke records a manuscript variant at each of two verses, a lie for knowledge in the seventh and direct his way for understand his way in the eighth, confessing that he cannot conjecture how the first arose; he says the learned have brought the ninth verse into embarrassments out of which they could not extricate it and doubts anyone will improve on the received version; he describes the whole animal nature suffering under spiritual sorrow while a stranger cannot intermeddle; and he recalls persecutors who thought that burning others was doing God service. Wesley makes the wit of ungodly men employed only in finding out ways of deceiving, and keeps the griefs and joys of the heart shut up in a man’s self.

Keil and Delitzsch deny that the second half of the seventh verse assigns a motive, since that would have required a different particle, and explain the compound as marking a distance from the sphere of vision at which the object is still in sight; they refuse to read the folly of the eighth verse as self-deceit, three old versions notwithstanding, because the word carries the notion of malicious fraud; they render the ninth as the sacrificial offering of fools mocketh, rejecting two proposed senses of the verb and taking the offering as a penitential work; and they assign the firm house to the wicked and the fragile tent to the upright, calling the rightness of the twelfth verse a phantom. Ellicott fixes the departure of the seventh verse at the point where no good can be done, instances Samuel and Saul, offers both that sin mocks fools and that the sin offering mocks them, and names the Son of Man as the one who can sympathise perfectly.

debates: What does the second half of the seventh verse do? Keil and Delitzsch deny it gives a reason for departing, against two early translators who read it as a purpose clause.

How should the ninth verse be rendered? Keil and Delitzsch read the sacrificial offering of fools mocketh and reject two interpreters’ senses of the verb; Clarke holds that the learned have only embarrassed the verse and that the received version is as near as any.

Is the folly of the eighth verse self-deception or fraud against others? Keil and Delitzsch insist on fraud, against three old versions that render it error; Ellicott and Wesley agree that it aims at cheating others.
outliers: Clarke reports manuscript variants at two consecutive verses, a lie for knowledge and direct his way for understand his way.
Ellicott names the Son of Man as the one exception to the rule that no stranger can share another’s bitterness or joy, noting that he could still join the marriage feast.
Keil and Delitzsch observe the reversal of expectation in the eleventh verse, where the solid house belongs to the wicked and the fragile tent to the upright.
themes: when to leave a fool’s company
practical wisdom against speculation
the mock at sin or the offering of fools
a bitterness no stranger can enter
the house that falls and the tent that flourishes

13.pericope_label: Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful: the backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways: the simple believeth every word: a wise man feareth and departeth from evil: he that is soon angry dealeth foolishly: the simple inherit folly

schools.summary: Henry reads the thirteenth verse as proof that carnal mirth is mad, since sinners under conviction dissemble grief by a forced mirth and even real merriment carries an alloy, spiritual joy being seated in the soul while the joy of the hypocrite is but from the teeth outward; he makes the backslider’s filling an eternal surfeit upon his sins; he lists the marks of credulity and the prudent man’s weighing of witness and testimony; and he judges the hasty man pitiable because his fit is soon over, while the man of wicked devices who waits for revenge is odious and there is no fence against him.

Gill instances Belshazzar merry at his feast until he saw the writing on the wall, says the backslider will have his bellyful of his own ways, holds that the wise man’s departure from evil springs from a sense of goodness rather than the fear of punishment that one rabbi assigned, and makes the folly of the simple natural and hereditary, received from their ancestors and retained as a patrimony.

Clarke answers a set of questions on the backslider in order, identifying him as one who once walked in religion and has withdrawn, once fought and has retreated or joined the enemy, once belonged to the saints and now sits in the synagogue of Satan, and distinguishing the backslider in heart from the man overcome by temptation; he explains the phrase for soon angry as short of nostrils, since anger contracts the nose towards the eyes; and he pairs caution with confidence, the one leading the wise man from sin and the other leading him to God. Wesley makes the prudent man consider not what others say but what he ought to do.

Keil and Delitzsch ground the sadness of the thirteenth verse in a disquiet native to every heart, which returns the more intensely the more it has been suppressed; they define the good man by self-sacrificing love as motive; they refuse to render the simple man’s belief as belief in every thing, since word and faith are correlates; they reject the renderings that make the fool merely over-confident, the verb meaning everywhere to fall into extreme anger; they answer Ewald’s correction of the seventeenth verse; and they canvass and reject three senses for the crowning word of the eighteenth. Ellicott takes the sadness in laughter as God teaching that only he can satisfy the soul, says the backslider gets swine’s husks instead of food fit for God’s children, and compares the folly of the simple to weeds in unoccupied soil.

debates: Does the seventeenth verse contrast well? Ewald thought not and corrected the text so that the man of consideration smooths his soul; Keil and Delitzsch answer that the received text is good Hebrew and that the phrase need not be taken in a good sense.
What does the fool do in the sixteenth verse? Keil and Delitzsch reject over-confidence and headlong rushing alike, since the verb everywhere means to fall into extreme anger.

How should the crowning of the prudent be rendered? Keil and Delitzsch canvass an Arabic root for abundance, a sense of waiting that produced two ancient versions, and a sense of encompassing, and find each too weak.
outliers: Clarke sets out the backslider in a numbered catechism, asking who he is, who the backslider in heart is, and what his own ways are.
Clarke derives the phrase for soon angry from the nostrils, contracted and drawn up towards the eyes in anger.
Henry contrasts the crackling of thorns under a pot with joy seated in the soul, and calls the hypocrite’s joy a thing from the teeth outward.
themes: sorrow that survives laughter
the backslider anatomised
believing every word against proving it
fear as self-mistrusting reserve
the hasty man and the cold one

19.pericope_label: The evil bow before the good: the poor is hated even of his own neighbour: he that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: do they not err that devise evil: in all labour there is profit: the crown of the wise is their riches

schools.summary: Henry allows that the wicked are brought low and forced to beg while good men are enabled to give even to the evil, since where God grants life we must not deny a livelihood, and looks forward to the foolish virgins begging oil of the wise; he calls fair-weather friends swallow-friends, gone in winter, and draws the comfort that God will not desert us when we are poor; he places the despiser among those who set a neighbour with the dogs of their flock; and he sums the labour proverb as working without talking making men rich and talking without working making them poor.

Gill reports a rabbi who referred the bowing of the evil to a future glory and finds only scattered instances so far, Haman before Mordecai and heathen emperors before Constantine; he observes that the same man is respected or disrespected as he is in affluence or want, and that this holds of poverty in understanding as well as in purse; he notes that two old versions read the twenty-first verse of despising the poor; and he keeps the ploughing image, that devisers of evil sow their mischief and expect a fine harvest.

Clarke keeps the nineteenth verse literal, with those who have wasted their substance begging at the gates of benevolent men; he quotes two Latin authors on friends who are like swallows, present in the festive season and gone when the cold drives them away; he calls contempt for a natural blemish cruel, since a man is not the author of his own imperfections and would not retain them if he could; and he holds that a man of words is seldom a man of deeds. Wesley adds that the fool’s folly is not cured but made worse by his riches.

Keil and Delitzsch make the good that which has love for its principle and must at last hold the supremacy, and picture the fallen posting themselves at the entrance of the righteous man’s house; they call the hatred of the poor the old history daily repeating itself and quote a Latin poet on fair-weather friendship; they deny that contempt here means speaking contemptuously in a man’s presence, confessing that no German or English word answers to it; they refuse Hitzig’s two emendations at the twenty-second verse; they trace the word for gain to a root meaning stretched out long; and they reject the reading of prudence for riches at the twenty-fourth. Ellicott rests the certainty of the retribution on the tense and observes that a rich fool displays his folly the more from a conspicuous position.

debates: Should the twenty-second verse be emended? Hitzig proposed both to double the participle so that it means plotters and to alter the verb; Keil and Delitzsch refuse both and keep the ploughing sense beside that of fabricating.
Is the crown of the wise their riches or their prudence? Keil and Delitzsch reject the second reading, since the point is that riches coming to a man who already has wisdom heighten its influence.

When do the evil bow before the good? Gill reports a rabbi referring it to a future glory, Clarke and Henry find it in present beggary, and Ellicott rests its certainty on the tense though it may be long delayed.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch confess that no German or English expression completely answers to the kind of contempt named in the twenty-first verse.
Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch independently quote the same Latin lines on the many friends of the prosperous man, and Clarke adds the comparison of false friends to swallows.
Keil and Delitzsch note that a long run of proverbs here is bound together by key-words beginning with one letter.
themes: the bowing of the evil, now or hereafter
swallow-friends and the dark side of human nature
contempt that insults rather than mocks
ploughing mischief and expecting a harvest
riches as a crown upon wisdom

25.pericope_label: A true witness delivereth souls: in the fear of the Lord is strong confidence: the fear of the Lord is a fountain of life: in the multitude of people is the king’s honour: he that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: a sound heart is the life of the flesh

schools.summary: Henry says the good names of the innocent are as dear to them as their lives, that a man of integrity will venture the displeasure of the greatest to bring truth to light, and that a nation should detect and punish false witness since truth is the cement of society; he observes that the children of religious parents often fare the better for their instruction and example; he calls the twenty-eighth verse two maxims in politics and urges mild government and the encouragement of trade and husbandry; he makes meekness wisdom and the hasty man all fire and tow; and he says people grow fat with good humour while the envious spirit makes the countenance pale.

Gill notes that the true witness delivers souls in the plural, a whole family or more, and that an old version adds the words from evils; he hears the well of living water springing up to everlasting life in the fountain of the twenty-seventh verse; he reads the crowded kingdom as a sign of clemency and righteousness with liberty and property enjoyed; and he prefers for the last verse the sense of a healing heart, humane and friendly, which is the life of others as well as of its own flesh.

Clarke holds that the fear of God is highly consistent with the strongest confidence in his mercy, gives the Hebrew of the fountain of life as the vein of lives and takes it for an allusion to the great artery carrying blood from the heart to the extremities, urges that every state should promote marriage, disgrace celibacy, bar bachelors from public employment after a certain age and banish the religious houses as having contributed more to vice than virtue, explains the hasty man as the short of spirit who is literally short of breath, and reduces the sound heart to a healthy state of the blood. Wesley has the fool’s folly lifted like a banner.

Keil and Delitzsch set the twenty-fifth verse in a criminal process where a conscientious tongue saves lives, and decline to carry its verb forward into the second line; they refuse to make the fear of God itself the thing relied on, since it is not faith but the object faith lays hold of that is the rock; they give the root of the king’s honour as swelling or enlarging and explain the contrasting term as denoting ruin here though it means without or groundless elsewhere; they parse the slow man as one who shuts anger long out and the hasty as short in respect of time; and they picture the quiet heart as a calm water-mirror. Ellicott asks whose children find the refuge, hears the man of rest in the twenty-eighth verse, and offers two senses for exalting folly.

debates: Whose children have the refuge of the twenty-sixth verse? Ellicott allows both the children of the man who fears the Lord and the children of God who look up to him as a father; Henry takes the first.
What is relied on in the fear of the Lord? Keil and Delitzsch deny that the fear itself is the ground, holding that the rock is the object which faith lays hold of rather than anything subjective.
What does it mean to exalt folly? Ellicott offers both bringing it into view and carrying it off as a portion; Wesley makes it a banner lifted up.
outliers: Clarke draws a state policy out of the twenty-eighth verse, urging marriage, the disgracing of celibacy, the barring of bachelors from public employment, and the banishing of religious houses.
Clarke reads the fountain of life as a physiological figure, the vein of lives answering to the great artery from the heart.
Henry argues that a nation should punish false witness because truth is the cement of society.
themes: the tongue that saves a life
fear resting on its object, not itself
a populous kingdom as a king’s honour
anger deferred and anger short-winded
the quiet heart as a still water-mirror

31.pericope_label: He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: the wicked is driven away in his wickedness: wisdom resteth in the heart of him that hath understanding: righteousness exalteth a nation: the king’s favour is toward a wise servant

schools.summary: Henry argues that God made the poor man and appointed him his lot, so that dealing hardly with any because they are poor reflects on God as having laid them low; he makes the wicked man cleave so closely to the world that he must be driven out of it, while sin cleaves so closely to him that it goes with him into another world; he calls modesty the badge of wisdom, since wisdom must rest in the heart and not swim in the head while fools bring their little knowledge in by head and shoulders; he notes that alms are sometimes called righteousness; and he says that in a well-ordered government no man’s services are neglected to please a party or a favourite.

Gill itemises the oppression of the poor as scoffing at a man for his poverty, vexatious lawsuits, withholding wages or refusing relief; he has the wicked driven from the world as a beast is driven, sore against his will, where the righteous depart and desire to depart; he makes the heart a treasury where wisdom lies undisturbed; and he takes the righteousness that exalts a nation as justice administered by the government and practised by subjects towards one another.

Clarke places the poor in the order of God as part of the inhabitants of the earth, given for the exercise of compassionate feelings without which men had been little better than brutes; he addresses the dying wicked man directly, that he will not go off but God will drive him; he refuses the rendering that sin is a reproach to any people and would have it that mercy is a sin-offering for the people, citing a Latin and a Greek version and holding that a national disposition to mercy appears before God as a continual sin-offering though it atones for nothing; and he holds that a king needs a minister of deep sense and merciful disposition, since most wars are occasioned by bad ministers, men of blood. Wesley says the poor man bears his Maker’s image and that fools publish their knowledge in all times and companies.

Keil and Delitzsch note the chiasmus of the predicates in the thirty-first verse; they render the thirty-second as the overthrow of the godless when misfortune befalls him, and report that the old versions changed his death to his uprightness for the sake of parallelism, answering that no word of Scripture commends self-righteousness so contradictorily; they survey and reject the attempts made on the second line of the thirty-third verse, allowing only the interpreter who adheres to the ascertained meaning of the words; and they distinguish three Hebrew words for a people, as a mass of common origin, as a confederation under common law, and as a multitude. Ellicott would render the thirty-first verse so that he who has mercy on the poor honours him, takes the wicked to be overthrown in his misfortune with none to aid him, and makes wisdom the subject of both halves of the thirty-third verse, since the fool cannot keep to himself anything he thinks he knows.

debates: What stands in the second line of the thirty-third verse? Keil and Delitzsch report that the old versions insert a negative, a paraphrase supplies the word folly, and two scholars make wisdom lost or reeling, and reject all of these for the plain sense that Ellicott also reaches.

Should the thirty-second verse read in his death or in his uprightness? Keil and Delitzsch keep the received text against the old versions, since the verb never denotes self-confidence and no word of Scripture commends self-righteousness in that manner.
Is sin a reproach to the people? Clarke says no, and would render the line that mercy is a sin-offering for the people, against the common version that Henry and Gill both assume.
outliers: Clarke turns the last verse into advice on ministers of state, holding that most wars are occasioned by bad ministers, men of blood.
Keil and Delitzsch give a short lexicon of the Hebrew words for a people, distinguishing origin, law and number.
Henry observes that alms are sometimes called righteousness, so that the righteousness which exalts a nation includes its charity to strangers.
themes: oppression of the poor as an affront to God
driven out of the world against the will
wisdom that rests instead of showing itself
mercy as a nation’s sin-offering
the minister a king should choose
